paper_context.research_question: How can overly-specific extractions be reduced in Open Information Extraction (OIE) systems without producing uninformative or inaccurate results?
contribution_type: Novel Method for Open Information Extraction Minimization
Enhanced Annotation Scheme for OIE Extractions
main_claims: MinIE effectively reduces overly-specific OIE extractions by identifying and removing specific parts and representing contextual information (polarity, modality, attribution, quantities) via suitable annotations.
MinIE achieves competitive or higher factual precision and recall compared to most prior OIE systems.
MinIE produces significantly shorter extractions than prior systems.
MinIE's annotations, particularly for negative polarity, help alleviate the problem of absence of negative evidence for reasoning with OIE extractions.
expected_evaluation_dimensions: Recall (total number of extractions, non-redundant extractions).
Minimality/Length of extractions (mean word count and standard deviation).
Effectiveness of different minimization modes (Safe, Frequency, Collocations, Aggressive).
Comparison against state-of-the-art OIE systems (ClausIE, OLLIE, Stanford OIE).

extracted_claims.claim_label: MinIE reduces overly-specific extractions via removal and annotation
extracted_claims.claim_text: MinIE effectively reduces overly-specific OIE extractions by identifying and removing specific parts and representing contextual information (polarity, modality, attribution, quantities) via suitable annotations.
evidence: At its heart, MinIE rewrites OIE extractions by (1) identifying and removing parts that are considered overly specific; (2) representing information about polarity, modality, attribution, and quantities with suitable annotations instead of in the actual extraction.
MinIE detects negations in the relation, removes them from the extraction, and adds a “negative polarity” (-) annotation.

extracted_claims.claim_label: MinIE achieves competitive/higher factual precision and recall
extracted_claims.claim_text: MinIE achieves competitive or higher factual precision and recall compared to most prior OIE systems.
evidence: We conducted an experimental study with several real-world datasets and found that MinIE achieves competitive or higher precision and recall than most prior systems...
We found that Stanford OIE had the lowest factual precision throughout... ClausIE and OLLIE had similar factual precision. Note that MinIE-S had higher precision than ClausIE.
uncertainty_flags: MinIE sometimes fell behind prior systems in terms of the total number of extractions. We found that those prior system can output a large number of redundant extractions; if redundant extractions were discounted, MinIE was competitive.

extracted_claims.claim_text: MinIE produces significantly shorter extractions than prior systems.
evidence: MinIE... at the same time producing much shorter extractions.
We found that the various modes of MinIE produced much shorter extractions than prior systems...

We observed that all modes of MinIE achieved significantly smaller extractions than ClausIE (its underlying OIE system), and that the average extraction length indeed dropped as we used more aggressive modes.
uncertainty_flags: Only MinIE-A produced shorter extractions than Stanford OIE. The main reason for the short extraction length of Stanford OIE is its aggressive creation of (shorter) redundant extractions.

extracted_claims.claim_label: Negative polarity annotations alleviate absence of negative evidence
extracted_claims.claim_text: MinIE's annotations, particularly for negative polarity, help alleviate the problem of absence of negative evidence for reasoning with OIE extractions.
evidence: To the best of our knowledge, MinIE is the first OIE system to produce such negative-polarity extractions. The absence of negative evidence is a major concern for reasoning with OIE extractions—e.g., (Dong et al., 2014) proposes to use a “local closed world assumption” and (Riedel et al., 2013; Petroni et al., 2015) use “negative sampling” methods—, and MinIE’s annotations help to alleviate this problem.

extracted_claims.claim_label: MinIE's relation enrichment produces more informative relations
extracted_claims.claim_text: MinIE's approach to enriching relations (based on ClausIE and Fader et al., 2011) produces more informative relations than ClausIE's original approach.
evidence: In MinIE, we follow (Fader et al., 2011) and try to produce more informative relations. To do so, we aim to decide which constituents of the input sentence should be pushed into the relation.
This allows us, for example, to handle cases with multiple adverbials or with adverbials that do not start with a preposition.
uncertainty_flags: Note that the relations produced in this step may sometimes be considered overly specific; they will be minimized further in subsequent steps.
As this example indicates, this rewrite is somewhat unsatisfying; further exploration is an interesting direction for future work.

extracted_claims.claim_label: Basic minimization steps are domain-independent and safe
extracted_claims.claim_text: MinIE's basic minimization steps (polarity, modality, attribution, quantities) are domain-independent and considered safe to use.
evidence: The basic minimization step of MinIE detects and eliminates information about polarity (Sec. 5.1), modality (Sec. 5.2), attribution (Sec. 5.3), and quantities (Sec. 5.4). Our focus is on methods that are both domain-independent and (considered) safe to use.

extracted_claims.claim_text: MinIE's safe mode (MinIE-S) only drops words considered universally safe to drop when applied to basic extractions.

extracted_claims.claim_text: The various minimization modes of MinIE (Safe, Frequency, Collocations, Aggressive) offer different levels of aggressiveness, resulting in varying extraction lengths and precision.

The modes differ in the amount of minimizations being applied and which additional resources are being used.

We observed that all modes of MinIE achieved significantly smaller extractions than ClausIE... and that the average extraction length indeed dropped as we used more aggressive modes. For MinIE, the factual precision dropped as expected when we use more aggressive modes.

extracted_claims.claim_text: MinIE's aggressive mode (MinIE-A) achieved higher precision than Stanford OIE.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Overly-specific extractions are a key challenge in OIE that needs to be addressed to produce informative and accurate results.
supporting_evidence: A key challenge in OIE is to avoid overly-specific extractions— while simultaneously producing informative and accurate results—when sentences get more complex.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If overly-specific extractions are not a significant problem, the core motivation and utility of MinIE's minimization techniques are diminished.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Representing contextual information (polarity, modality, attribution, quantities) as annotations rather than within the extraction itself retains original meaning and is beneficial for downstream tasks.
supporting_evidence: To retain the original meaning to the extent possible, MinIE provides suitable annotations for each extraction.

Some annotations (such as polarity) are crucial to correctly represent the extraction, others (such as original relation) give additional information about which parts have been removed during minimization.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If annotations are not adequately utilized by downstream applications or if they fail to preserve the original meaning, the minimized extractions could be uninformative or inaccurate.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: ClausIE is a suitable underlying OIE system for MinIE due to its constituent separation, clause type detection, and state-of-the-art status.
supporting_evidence: While the techniques employed by MinIE can in principle be integrated into any OIE system, we built MinIE on top of ClausIE (Del Corro and Gemulla, 2013). We chose ClausIE because (1) it separates the identification of the constituents of the extractions from the generation of propositions, (2) it detects clause types, which are also useful for MinIE, and (3) it is a state-of-the-art OIE system.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If ClausIE's foundational capabilities are flawed or not truly state-of-the-art, MinIE's performance might be limited by its base system, regardless of its minimization techniques.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The chosen lexicon for negation words (no, not, never, none) is sufficient to detect most relevant negations in relations for basic minimization.
supporting_evidence: We detect negations using a small lexicon of negation words (consisting of the words no, not, never, none). Whenever a word from the lexicon is detected, it is dropped from the relation and the triple is annotated with negative polarity (-) and the negation word.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If the lexicon is incomplete, many negations will be missed, leading to less minimized extractions and potentially incorrect interpretations if the negation is not explicitly handled by downstream systems.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Restricting negation detection to 'easy cases' (words in relation, not subject/argument) is a safe approach in the absence of domain knowledge, even if it misses some negations.
supporting_evidence: We consider such advanced minimizations too dangerous to use in the absence of domain knowledge. Generally, negation detection is a hard problem and involves questions such as negation scope resolution, focus detection, and double negation (Blanco and Moldovan, 2011). MinIE does not address these problems, but restricts attention to the easy cases.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If the 'easy cases' assumption is too restrictive, MinIE might fail to minimize many valid negations, reducing its effectiveness. If the 'dangerous' advanced minimizations are actually safe in many contexts, MinIE is unnecessarily conservative.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The lexicon for possibility-indicating words and infinitive verb phrases is sufficient to detect relevant modalities for basic minimization.
supporting_evidence: To find such evidence, MinIE searches the relation for (1) modal verbs such as may or can, (2) possibility-indicating words, and (3) certain infinitive verb phrases. For (2) and (3), we make use of a small domain-indepependent lexicon. Our lexicon is based on the lexicon of (Saurı́ and Pustejovsky, 2012) and the words in the corresponding WordNet synsets.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: An incomplete lexicon would lead to missed modality annotations, potentially misrepresenting the factuality of extractions.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The domain-independent dictionary of relations indicating attributions (e.g., say or believe) is sufficient for identifying attribution suppliers.
supporting_evidence: MinIE searches for extractions that contain entire clauses as arguments. We then compare the relation against a domain-independent dictionary of relations indicating attributions (e.g., say or believe).
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If the dictionary is not comprehensive, many attributions will be missed, reducing the richness of MinIE's annotations.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Replacing quantities with a placeholder 'Q' and annotating them unifies extractions that only differ in quantities, which is a desirable minimization goal.
supporting_evidence: Whenever we detect a quantity, we replace it by a placeholder Q and add an annotation with the original quantity. The goal of this step is to unify extractions that only differ in quantities.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If unifying extractions based solely on quantity differences is not always desirable, or if the placeholder 'Q' loses crucial information for certain applications, this minimization could be detrimental.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Named entities are universally stable subconstituents and should always be fully retained during minimization.
supporting_evidence: In all of MinIE’s modes, named entites are considered stable subconstituents.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If parts of named entities are sometimes overly specific or if their full retention prevents optimal minimization in certain contexts, this assumption could hinder the system's performance.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The specific rules for dropping words in Safe Mode (determiners, possessive pronouns, adverbs modifying verb, adjectives/adverbials modifying persons) are 'universally safe' when applied to basic extractions.
supporting_evidence: MinIE’s safe mode only drops word which we consider universally safe to drop.

We consider it safe, however, when applied to basic extractions. In particular, all determiners, pronouns, and adverbs indicating negation, modality, or quantities are already processed during basic minimization and are consequently retained in annotations.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If these rules inadvertently remove crucial information in some contexts, even after basic minimization, the 'safe' mode could produce uninformative or inaccurate extractions.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The external dictionaries (WordNet, Wiktionary multi-word expressions) used for MinIE-C provide a sufficiently comprehensive set of domain-independent collocations.
supporting_evidence: In MinIE’s collocations mode, D is provided externally and contains a set of collocations. In our experimental study, we included all multi-word expressions from WordNet and Wiktionary, which we consider domain-independent.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If these dictionaries are incomplete, MinIE-C might incorrectly break up valid collocations, leading to less precise or meaningful extractions. This is acknowledged as a source of error.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Frequency thresholds (e.g., ≥ 10) for subjects, relations, and arguments in MinIE-F accurately identify 'sufficiently frequent' constituents that are not considered overly specific.
supporting_evidence: In MinIE’s frequency mode, we process the entire corpus using the safe mode and additionally include all frequent (e.g., frequency ≥ 10) subjects, relations, and arguments into D. This lexical constraint is inspired by (Fader et al., 2011); the rationale is that everything sufficiently frequent is not considered overly specific.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: An inappropriate frequency threshold could either retain overly specific infrequent terms or remove genuinely important but less frequent terms, impacting precision and minimality.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Errors in dependency parsing are the main source of errors in MinIE-S, implying that improving parsing would significantly improve MinIE's performance.
supporting_evidence: For all modes, errors in dependency parsing transfer over to errors in MinIE, which we believe is the main source of errors in MinIE-S.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If other error sources are equally or more significant, focusing solely on parsing improvements might not yield the expected performance gains for MinIE-S.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The definition of 'redundant extraction' (a triple t1 is redundant if it appears as a subsequence in another triple t2 from the same sentence) is an appropriate measure for evaluating redundancy.
supporting_evidence: For simplicity, we consider a triple t1 redundant if it appears as subsequence in some other triple t2 produced by the same extractor from the same sentence (e.g., extraction 5 in Tab. 1 is redundant given extraction 6).
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If this definition of redundancy is too simplistic or doesn't capture all forms of redundancy, the reported 'non-redundant extractions' metric might not accurately reflect the true uniqueness of extractions.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Mean word count and standard deviation are appropriate proxies for minimality of extractions.
supporting_evidence: We also determined the mean word count per extraction (µ) and its standard deviation (σ); we use these numbers as a proxy for minimality.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Minimality might involve more than just word count (e.g., semantic density, conciseness without loss of meaning). Relying solely on word count might not fully capture the quality of minimization.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The chosen datasets (NYT-10k, NYT, Wiki) are representative for evaluating OIE system performance in terms of precision, recall, and minimality.
supporting_evidence: We used as datasets (1) a random sample of 10,000 sentences from the New York Times Annotated Corpus (NYT-10k), (2) a random sample of 200 sentences from the same corpus (NYT), and (3) a random sample of 200 sentences from Wikipedia (Wiki). Datasets NYT and Wiki were used in the evaluation of ClausIE and NestIE.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If these datasets are not representative of typical OIE use cases or contain biases, the reported performance metrics might not generalize to other domains or text types.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The labeling guidelines for factual precision (entailed by clause, factuality annotations considered) and attribution precision (attribution present in annotation, fact triple correct) are robust and capture the intended correctness.
supporting_evidence: We labeled every extraction of NYT and Wiki with two labels: one for the triple and one for the attribution. A triple is labeled as correct if it is entailed by its corresponding clause; here factuality annotations are taken into account. ... The attribution is labeled incorrect if there is an attribution which is neither present in the triple nor in the attribution annotation. We only label attribution when the fact triple is labeled correct. Further details can be found in the labelling guidelines.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If the labeling guidelines are ambiguous, inconsistent, or do not align with the true definition of correctness for OIE extractions and attributions, the reported precision scores could be misleading.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript introduces MinIE, an Open Information Extraction (OIE) system designed to address the problem of overly-specific extractions. The core argument is that by systematically identifying and removing overly-specific parts while simultaneously representing crucial contextual information (polarity, modality, attribution, quantities) through a novel annotation scheme, MinIE can produce shorter, more informative, and equally or more accurate extractions. The paper logically progresses from defining the problem and motivating the solution, through a detailed description of MinIE's architecture (built on ClausIE, with relation enrichment and implicit extractions), its 'basic' (safe, domain-independent) minimization steps, and its 'aggressive' configurable minimization modes (Safe, Frequency, Collocations, Aggressive). This methodological exposition is followed by an extensive experimental study comparing MinIE's performance against state-of-the-art OIE systems across various metrics (precision, recall, minimality, attribution accuracy). The results consistently support the claims of reduced extraction length and competitive precision, with a transparent discussion of error sources. The logical flow is clear, moving from problem to solution, implementation, and empirical validation.
logical_argument_graph: Problem Statement (Section 1): Existing OIE systems produce overly-specific extractions, hindering informativeness and accuracy, especially with complex sentences.
Proposed Solution (Section 1): Introduce MinIE, an OIE system that minimizes and annotates extractions to overcome this challenge.

Core Mechanisms (Section 1, 5): MinIE operates by (1) identifying and removing overly specific parts from extractions, and (2) representing contextual information (polarity, modality, attribution, quantities) via suitable annotations to retain original meaning.
Architectural Foundation (Section 3): MinIE is built on ClausIE, leveraging its constituent separation and clause type detection capabilities as a robust base.

Input Processing (Section 4): Initial extractions are prepared through two steps: (1) Relation Enrichment (Section 4.1) to produce more informative relations by incorporating additional constituents, and (2) Implicit Extractions (Section 4.2) to generate non-verb-mediated facts used as signals for subsequent minimization.

Basic Minimization (Section 5): A set of 'safe' and domain-independent transformations are applied: (1) Polarity (Section 5.1) by detecting and annotating negations, (2) Modality (Section 5.2) by identifying and annotating possibility, (3) Attribution (Section 5.3) by extracting and annotating information suppliers, and (4) Quantities (Section 5.4) by replacing numerical/quantifier phrases with a placeholder and annotating the original quantity.

Aggressive Minimization Modes (Section 6): Beyond basic minimization, MinIE offers configurable modes with increasing aggressiveness, all respecting 'stable subconstituents' (e.g., named entities): (1) Safe Mode (MinIE-S, Section 6.1) drops universally safe words, (2) Frequency Mode (MinIE-F, Section 6.2) uses corpus frequency to retain common constituents, (3) Collocations Mode (MinIE-C, Section 6.2) leverages external dictionaries for multi-word expressions, and (4) Aggressive Mode (MinIE-A, Section 6.3) serves as a baseline by dropping most modifiers.

Experimental Evaluation (Section 7): An empirical study is conducted to validate MinIE's performance. (1) Setup (Section 7.1) details datasets (NYT-10k, NYT, Wiki), baselines (ClausIE, OLLIE, Stanford OIE), labeling process, and metrics (recall, factual precision, attribution precision, minimality/length). (2) Extraction Statistics (Section 7.2) show MinIE produces significantly shorter extractions and is competitive in non-redundant recall. (3) Precision (Section 7.3) demonstrates MinIE's competitive or higher factual precision, with MinIE-S outperforming ClausIE and MinIE-A outperforming Stanford OIE. (4) Error Analysis (Section 7.4) identifies primary error sources as dependency parsing, incomplete collocation dictionaries, and Named Entity Recognizer (NER) errors.

Conclusion (Section 8): The paper concludes that minimized, annotated extractions represent a promising direction for OIE, with MinIE serving as a significant step. Future work is outlined, including additional annotation types and improved minimization techniques.

strengths.title: Comprehensive and Modular Minimization Strategy
strengths.description: MinIE presents a well-structured, multi-stage approach to OIE minimization, starting with 'safe' basic annotations and progressing to more aggressive, configurable modes. This modularity allows for flexible application depending on the desired trade-off between minimality and precision, which is a significant practical advantage.
evidence: MinIE supports multiple minimization modes, which differ in their aggressiveness.

The basic minimization step of MinIE detects and eliminates information about polarity (Sec. 5.1), modality (Sec. 5.2), attribution (Sec. 5.3), and quantities (Sec. 5.4). Our focus is on methods that are both domain-independent and (considered) safe to use.

MinIE then rewrites each input extraction to a basic extraction by detecting and eliminating information about polarity (Sec. 5.1), modality (Sec. 5.2), attribution (Sec. 5.3), and quantities (Sec. 5.4). To further minimize basic extractions, MinIE can be run in various modes (Sec. 6) with increasing levels of aggressiveness: MinIE-S(afe), MinIE-F(requency), MinIE-C(ollocations), and MinIE-A(ggressive).

strengths.title: Novel Annotation Scheme for Contextual Information
strengths.description: The introduction of explicit annotations for polarity, modality, attribution, and quantities, particularly negative polarity, is a novel and valuable contribution. This addresses a known limitation in OIE by retaining crucial contextual information that would otherwise be lost during minimization, thereby enhancing the utility of extractions for downstream reasoning tasks.
evidence: To retain the original meaning to the extent possible, MinIE provides suitable annotations for each extraction.

MinIE detects negations in the relation, removes them from the extraction, and adds a “negative polarity” (-) annotation. In fact, MinIE considers the relations was born on and was not born on equivalent up to polarity. To the best of our knowledge, MinIE is the first OIE system to produce such negative-polarity extractions.

The absence of negative evidence is a major concern for reasoning with OIE extractions—e.g., (Dong et al., 2014) proposes to use a “local closed world assumption” and (Riedel et al., 2013; Petroni et al., 2015) use “negative sampling” methods—, and MinIE’s annotations help to alleviate this problem.

strengths.title: Strong Empirical Validation of Core Claims
strengths.description: The experimental study provides robust evidence that MinIE effectively achieves its primary goals: producing significantly shorter extractions while maintaining competitive or even higher factual precision compared to several state-of-the-art OIE systems. The detailed comparison across different modes and baselines strengthens these claims.
evidence: We conducted an experimental study with several real-world datasets and found that the various modes of MinIE produced much shorter extractions than prior systems, while simultaneously achieving competitive or higher precision.

We observed that all modes of MinIE achieved significantly smaller extractions than ClausIE (its underlying OIE system), and that the average extraction length indeed dropped as we used more aggressive modes.

Note that MinIE-S had higher precision than ClausIE. Reasons include that MinIE-S produces additional high-precision implicit extractions, breaks up very long and thus error-prone extractions, and uses a different version of Stanford CoreNLP.
Surprisingly to us, even MinIE’s aggressive mode achieved higher precision than Stanford OIE.

strengths.title: Transparent Error Analysis
strengths.description: The paper includes a dedicated section for error analysis, transparently discussing the main sources of errors (dependency parsing, incomplete dictionaries for collocations, and Named Entity Recognizer errors). This self-awareness is crucial for understanding the system's limitations and provides clear directions for future improvements.
evidence: For all modes, errors in dependency parsing transfer over to errors in MinIE, which we believe is the main source of errors in MinIE-S.

For MinIE-C and MinIE-F, we sometimes drop adjectives which in fact form collocations (e.g., “assistant director”) with the noun they are modifying, but the collocation is not present in the dictionary and thus broken up. This problem can be addressed by using richer collocation dictionaries.

Another source of error stems from the named-entity recognizer (e.g., the first word of the named entity Personal Ensign was not recognized so that MinIE incorrectly extracts (”Ensign”, ”is”, ”Personal”)).

concerns.title: Reliance on Lexicon Completeness for Basic Minimization
concerns.description: The effectiveness of MinIE's basic minimization steps (polarity, modality, attribution, quantities) heavily relies on the completeness and accuracy of the underlying lexicons and dictionaries (Assumptions A4, A6, A7). An incomplete lexicon could lead to missed minimizations or incorrect annotations, potentially reducing the system's overall utility and the richness of its output. While acknowledged for collocations, this applies broadly to all lexicon-based basic steps.

For (2) and (3) [possibility-indicating words and infinitive verb phrases], we make use of a small domain-indepependent lexicon. Our lexicon is based on the lexicon of (Saurı́ and Pustejovsky, 2012) and the words in the corresponding WordNet synsets.
We then compare the relation against a domain-independent dictionary of relations indicating attributions (e.g., say or believe).

For MinIE-C and MinIE-F, we sometimes drop adjectives which in fact form collocations (e.g., “assistant director”) with the noun they are modifying, but the collocation is not present in the dictionary and thus broken up. This problem can be addressed by using richer collocation dictionaries.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide a more detailed analysis of the coverage and potential limitations of the lexicons and dictionaries used for basic minimizations. Consider strategies for automatically expanding or validating these resources.

concerns.title: Limited Scope of Negation and Modality Detection
concerns.description: MinIE explicitly restricts its negation and modality detection to 'easy cases' (Assumption A5), avoiding complex linguistic phenomena like scope resolution, focus detection, and double negation. While a pragmatic choice for a domain-independent system, this design decision limits the system's ability to fully capture and annotate these crucial contextual elements in more nuanced sentences, potentially leaving valuable information unminimized or unannotated, thus reducing the overall effectiveness of these annotations.
evidence: We consider such advanced minimizations too dangerous to use in the absence of domain knowledge. Generally, negation detection is a hard problem and involves questions such as negation scope resolution, focus detection, and double negation (Blanco and Moldovan, 2011). MinIE does not address these problems, but restricts attention to the easy cases.
As with negation detection, MinIE’s approach focuses on the easy cases and uses only the CT and PS levels. A more advanced approach is taken by (Saurı́ and Pustejovsky, 2012).
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Discuss the potential impact of this limitation on downstream tasks that rely on comprehensive factuality annotations. Consider outlining a roadmap for future work to address more complex cases, perhaps with a focus on specific high-impact scenarios.

concerns.title: Simplistic Definition of Redundant Extractions
concerns.description: The definition of 'redundant extraction' as a triple appearing as a subsequence in another triple from the same sentence (Assumption A14) is a simplification. This definition might not fully capture all forms of semantic redundancy, where two extractions convey the same core information but are syntactically different. This could potentially lead to an overestimation of the 'non-redundant' extractions for some systems, affecting the interpretation of recall metrics.
evidence: For simplicity, we consider a triple t1 redundant if it appears as subsequence in some other triple t2 produced by the same extractor from the same sentence (e.g., extraction 5 in Tab. 1 is redundant given extraction 6).
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Acknowledge the limitations of the subsequence-based redundancy definition more explicitly and discuss how a more semantically-aware redundancy metric might alter the recall comparisons. Perhaps provide examples where the current definition falls short.

concerns.title: Uncertainty in Attribution Precision Evaluation
concerns.description: The paper notes that attribution precision numbers should be taken 'with a grain of salt' due to sparse data in the samples. This caveat indicates a weakness in the evaluation of this specific annotation type, making it difficult to confidently assess the effectiveness and reliability of MinIE's attribution mechanism. The lack of robust evaluation data for this feature diminishes the strength of claims related to attribution.
evidence: As for attribution precision, most of the sentences in our samples did not contain attributions; these numbers should thus be taken with a grain of salt.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: If possible, conduct additional evaluation on a dataset specifically curated or augmented for attribution-rich sentences to provide a more reliable assessment of attribution precision. Alternatively, clearly state the implications of this data sparsity for interpreting the results.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper introduces MinIE, an Open Information Extraction (OIE) system designed to address the problem of overly-specific extractions. MinIE achieves this by (1) identifying and removing specific parts of extractions and (2) representing contextual information (polarity, modality, attribution, quantities) through a novel annotation scheme. The system is built on top of ClausIE and offers multiple minimization modes (Safe, Frequency, Collocations, Aggressive) with varying levels of aggressiveness. An experimental study evaluates MinIE against prior OIE systems (ClausIE, OLLIE, Stanford OIE) across metrics of factual precision, recall (total and non-redundant), and extraction minimality (mean word count). The core argument is that MinIE effectively produces shorter, more concise extractions while maintaining competitive or higher precision, and its annotations, particularly for negative polarity, address a critical gap in OIE for downstream reasoning.
logical_argument_graph: P1: Overly-specific extractions are a key challenge in OIE, leading to uninformative or inaccurate results (A1).
S1: MinIE proposes to reduce overly-specific extractions by removing specific parts and representing contextual information (polarity, modality, attribution, quantities) via annotations (C1, A2).
S2: MinIE is built on ClausIE, leveraging its constituent separation and clause type detection (A3).
S3: MinIE implements 'basic minimization' steps for polarity, modality, attribution, and quantities, which are designed to be domain-independent and safe (C6, A4, A5, A6, A7, A8).

S4: MinIE offers additional 'minimization modes' (Safe, Frequency, Collocations, Aggressive) that vary in aggressiveness, dropping words based on heuristic rules, frequency, or external dictionaries (C7, C8, A9, A10, A11, A12).
E1: An experimental study compares MinIE's modes against baselines (ClausIE, OLLIE, Stanford OIE) on NYT and Wiki datasets, measuring precision, recall, and minimality (A14, A15, A16, A17).
R1: MinIE produces significantly shorter extractions than prior systems, with length decreasing with more aggressive modes (C3).
R2: MinIE achieves competitive or higher factual precision and recall compared to most prior systems (C2, C9, C10, C11).
R3: MinIE's annotations, especially negative polarity, are novel and help alleviate the problem of absence of negative evidence for reasoning (C4).
R4: Errors in dependency parsing are believed to be the main source of errors for MinIE-S, while dictionary incompleteness affects MinIE-C/F (A13).

In MinIE’s collocations mode, D is provided externally and contains a set of collocations. In our experimental study, we included all multi-word expressions from WordNet and Wiktionary, which we consider domain-independent.

concerns.title: Insufficient Justification for 'Universally Safe' Minimization Rules
concerns.description: MinIE-S claims to drop words 'universally safe to drop' (C7, A10). While the paper explains that basic minimizations precede this and retain crucial information, the specific rules for dropping determiners, possessive pronouns, adverbs modifying verbs, and adjectives/adverbials modifying persons are presented as heuristic. There is no formal proof or extensive empirical validation across diverse linguistic contexts to substantiate the 'universal safety' claim, which is a strong assertion.
evidence: MinIE’s safe mode only drops word which we consider universally safe to drop.

We consider it safe, however, when applied to basic extractions. In particular, all determiners, pronouns, and adverbs indicating negation, modality, or quantities are already processed during basic minimization and are consequently retained in annotations.
We then drop all determiners, all possessive pronouns, all adverbs modifying the verb in the relation, and all adjectives and adverbials modifying persons.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide a more rigorous justification for the 'universal safety' of these rules, either through a formal linguistic analysis of their impact on meaning preservation or a comprehensive empirical study demonstrating their robustness across a wider range of corpora and domains.

concerns.title: Simplistic Definition of Redundancy and Minimality Metrics
concerns.description: The definition of 'redundant extraction' as a subsequence (A14) is simplistic and may not capture all forms of semantic redundancy. For example, 'Superman was born on Krypton' and 'Superman was born on his home planet Krypton' might be considered semantically redundant but not caught by a subsequence check if the latter is not a direct subsequence. Similarly, using only mean word count and standard deviation as a proxy for 'minimality' (A15) might overlook semantic conciseness or information density, which are more nuanced aspects of minimization quality.
evidence: For simplicity, we consider a triple t1 redundant if it appears as subsequence in some other triple t2 produced by the same extractor from the same sentence (e.g., extraction 5 in Tab. 1 is redundant given extraction 6).
We also determined the mean word count per extraction (µ) and its standard deviation (σ); we use these numbers as a proxy for minimality.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Explore more sophisticated metrics for redundancy (e.g., semantic similarity-based) and minimality (e.g., information content per word, human judgments of conciseness) to provide a more comprehensive evaluation of these aspects.

Without such an analysis, it's difficult to confirm the primary bottleneck or prioritize future improvements.

concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct a detailed error analysis, categorizing and quantifying the sources of errors for MinIE-S (and other modes) to empirically validate the claim about dependency parsing being the main source.

This indicates a known limitation in a core component of the system's initial processing. Additionally, MinIE currently does not handle nested extractions, which some prior systems (CSDIE, NestIE) address. This limits MinIE's scope and comparability in certain complex sentence structures.

comparable_works.source_trace: The concept of annotated OIE extractions was introduced by OLLIE (Schmitz et al., 2012). OLLIE uses two types of annotations: an attribution – describing the the supplier of the triple, and a clause modifier – describing clauses that modify the extraction. MinIE picks up the attribution annotation, and uses additional techniques to provide the attribution’s polarity and modality. The clause modifier is an alternative approach to CSD-IE’s notion of nested facts and not present in MinIE. specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript presents MinIE, an Open Information Extraction (OIE) system designed to address the challenge of overly-specific extractions while preserving or enhancing information content through a novel annotation scheme. MinIE systematically extends existing OIE paradigms by integrating a multi-stage minimization process, starting with 'basic' domain-independent and 'safe' transformations (polarity, modality, attribution, quantities) and progressing to more aggressive, lexicon- or frequency-driven modes. This approach refines prior work on lexical constraints (e.g., ReVerb) and dependency-based minimization (e.g., Stanford OIE) by offering a more granular and controlled spectrum of minimization strategies. Crucially, MinIE significantly reorganizes the representation of contextual information by introducing a richer set of annotations, notably negative polarity, which is explicitly identified as a novel contribution to OIE systems. This directly addresses a known limitation in reasoning with OIE extractions regarding the absence of negative evidence. While building upon an existing OIE system (ClausIE) and drawing inspiration from established techniques for relation enrichment (Fader et al., 2011) and factuality assessment (Saurí and Pustejovsky, 2012), MinIE's systematic integration of these elements into a configurable, performance-validated system represents a meaningful incremental advancement in the field.

strengths.title: Novel Conceptual Frame for OIE Output
strengths.description: The paper introduces a significant conceptual shift in OIE output representation by systematically separating core factual assertions from their contextual modifiers (polarity, modality, attribution, quantities) and representing the latter as explicit annotations. This re-framing moves beyond simply shortening extractions to providing a richer, more structured semantic representation for downstream consumption.
evidence: At its heart, MinIE rewrites OIE extractions by (1) identifying and removing parts that are considered overly specific; (2) representing information about polarity, modality, attribution, and quantities with suitable annotations instead of in the actual extraction.
MinIE’s factuality and quantity annotations have not been provided by existing OIE systems.

strengths.title: Disruptive Annotation of Negative Polarity
strengths.description: The explicit annotation of negative polarity is a particularly disruptive contribution. The paper correctly identifies the 'absence of negative evidence' as a major concern for reasoning with OIE extractions, and MinIE's approach directly addresses this by making negations first-class citizens in the output metadata. This could enable new forms of reasoning with OIE data.
evidence: To the best of our knowledge, MinIE is the first OIE system to produce such negative-polarity extractions. The absence of negative evidence is a major concern for reasoning with OIE extractions—e.g., (Dong et al., 2014) proposes to use a “local closed world assumption” and (Riedel et al., 2013; Petroni et al., 2015) use “negative sampling” methods—, and MinIE’s annotations help to alleviate this problem.

strengths.title: Principled Multi-Modal Minimization
strengths.description: The introduction of multiple, progressively aggressive minimization modes (Safe, Frequency, Collocations, Aggressive) provides a principled framework for users to choose the desired trade-off between minimality and information retention, based on their application needs. This systematic approach to managing specificity is a novel design choice.

prior_stage_inputs: The manuscript introduces MinIE, an Open Information Extraction (OIE) system designed to address the problem of overly-specific extractions. The core argument is that by systematically identifying and removing overly-specific parts while simultaneously representing crucial contextual information (polarity, modality, attribution, quantities) through a novel annotation scheme, MinIE can produce shorter, more informative, and equally or more accurate extractions. The paper logically progresses from defining the problem and motivating the solution, through a detailed description of MinIE's architecture (built on ClausIE, with relation enrichment and implicit extractions), its 'basic' (safe, domain-independent) minimization steps, and its 'aggressive' configurable minimization modes (Safe, Frequency, Collocations, Aggressive). This methodological exposition is followed by an extensive experimental study comparing MinIE's performance against state-of-the-art OIE systems across various metrics (precision, recall, minimality, attribution accuracy). The results consistently support the claims of reduced extraction length and competitive precision, with a transparent discussion of error sources. The logical flow is clear, moving from problem to solution, implementation, and empirical validation.

The paper introduces MinIE, an Open Information Extraction (OIE) system designed to address the problem of overly-specific extractions. MinIE achieves this by (1) identifying and removing specific parts of extractions and (2) representing contextual information (polarity, modality, attribution, quantities) through a novel annotation scheme. The system is built on top of ClausIE and offers multiple minimization modes (Safe, Frequency, Collocations, Aggressive) with varying levels of aggressiveness. An experimental study evaluates MinIE against prior OIE systems (ClausIE, OLLIE, Stanford OIE) across metrics of factual precision, recall (total and non-redundant), and extraction minimality (mean word count). The core argument is that MinIE effectively produces shorter, more concise extractions while maintaining competitive or higher precision, and its annotations, particularly for negative polarity, address a critical gap in OIE for downstream reasoning.

The manuscript presents MinIE, an Open Information Extraction (OIE) system designed to address the challenge of overly-specific extractions while preserving or enhancing information content through a novel annotation scheme. MinIE systematically extends existing OIE paradigms by integrating a multi-stage minimization process, starting with 'basic' domain-independent and 'safe' transformations (polarity, modality, attribution, quantities) and progressing to more aggressive, lexicon- or frequency-driven modes. This approach refines prior work on lexical constraints (e.g., ReVerb) and dependency-based minimization (e.g., Stanford OIE) by offering a more granular and controlled spectrum of minimization strategies. Crucially, MinIE significantly reorganizes the representation of contextual information by introducing a richer set of annotations, notably negative polarity, which is explicitly identified as a novel contribution to OIE systems. This directly addresses a known limitation in reasoning with OIE extractions regarding the absence of negative evidence. While building upon an existing OIE system (ClausIE) and drawing inspiration from established techniques for relation enrichment (Fader et al., 2011) and factuality assessment (Saurí and Pustejovsky, 2012), MinIE's systematic integration of these elements into a configurable, performance-validated system represents a meaningful incremental advancement in the field.

MinIE proposes a novel approach to Open Information Extraction (OIE) by addressing the problem of overly-specific extractions through a two-pronged strategy: systematic minimization of the core triple and comprehensive annotation of contextual information (polarity, modality, attribution, quantities). This represents a conceptual departure from traditional OIE systems that primarily focus on extracting verbose, surface-form triples. The system introduces a new output format where facts are concise, and their nuances are captured in structured metadata, aiming to improve utility for downstream reasoning tasks by providing explicit factuality cues, notably negative polarity, which is a significant innovation.
specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper introduces MinIE, an Open Information Extraction (OIE) system designed to reduce overly-specific extractions through a two-pronged approach: systematic removal of specific parts and comprehensive annotation of contextual information (polarity, modality, attribution, quantities). The core claims regarding MinIE's ability to produce significantly shorter extractions and achieve competitive or higher factual precision compared to most prior OIE systems are strongly supported by the empirical evaluation across various minimization modes. Specifically, MinIE-S demonstrates higher precision than ClausIE, and even MinIE-A outperforms Stanford OIE in precision while achieving greater minimality. The paper's assertion that negative polarity annotations help alleviate the problem of absence of negative evidence for reasoning is a plausible and novel contribution addressing a known challenge, though its direct empirical validation for downstream reasoning tasks is not provided within this work. Similarly, the claim of producing 'more informative relations' through enrichment is mechanistically described and implicitly supported by overall performance, but not quantified in isolation. The design principles of 'domain-independent' and 'safe' basic minimizations are stated and generally supported by the high precision of MinIE-S, although the 'universally safe' aspect relies on the completeness of lexicons and the scope of 'easy cases' as defined by the authors.

The paper acknowledges the difficulty of negation detection (A5) and the potential for errors in collocation modes (7.4), suggesting that 'safety' might be context-dependent.

concerns.title: Nuance in Recall Claim
concerns.description: The claim that MinIE achieves 'competitive or higher factual precision and recall' (C2) is partially overstated regarding raw recall. The paper acknowledges that MinIE sometimes fell behind prior systems in terms of total extractions, becoming competitive only when redundant extractions were discounted. human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary:
MinIE is an Open Information Extraction (OIE) system that addresses overly-specific extractions by systematically removing specific parts and representing contextual information (polarity, modality, attribution, quantities) via novel annotations. It empirically demonstrates significantly shorter extractions and competitive or higher factual precision compared to prior OIE systems, with its negative polarity annotations offering a new approach to handling negative evidence for reasoning.

Strengths:
- Systematic and configurable framework for OIE minimization, offering various modes with demonstrated trade-offs.
- Novel and comprehensive annotation scheme for contextual information (polarity, modality, attribution, quantities), particularly negative polarity, addressing a key challenge in OIE reasoning.
- Strong empirical validation showing significantly shorter extractions and competitive or superior factual precision against state-of-the-art systems.
- Transparent discussion of error sources and commitment to reproducibility (public code/data).

Limitations:
- The paper does not empirically demonstrate the utility of MinIE's novel annotations (e.g., negative polarity, modality) for downstream reasoning tasks, leaving their practical impact unvalidated.
- The completeness and generalizability of the 'small lexicons' and 'domain-independent dictionaries' used for basic minimizations and collocation detection are not fully established, which could limit the robustness and 'safety' of these processes across diverse domains.
- The claim of 'universally safe' minimization in MinIE-S is a strong assertion that lacks formal justification or extensive empirical validation across diverse linguistic contexts, potentially leading to unintended information loss.

Open Questions:
- How would downstream reasoning systems specifically consume and leverage MinIE's novel annotations (e.g., negative polarity, modality, attribution, quantities), and what empirical benefits would be expected in such applications?
- Can the authors provide a more detailed analysis of the coverage and potential limitations of the lexicons and dictionaries used for basic minimizations, or outline strategies for their automatic expansion/validation?
- What is the quantified contribution of different error sources (e.g., dependency parsing, NER, lexicon incompleteness) to MinIE's overall performance, particularly for MinIE-S?

Since the training data generated by the heuristic matching is often imperfect, multi- instance learning approaches (Riedel et al., 2010; Hoffmann et al., 2011; Surdeanu et al., 2012) have been developed to combat this problem. They fall short of learning extractors for ﬂuent facts such as sports results or travel and meetings by a person. Bootstrapping is another common extraction technique (Brin, 1999; Agichtein and Gravano, 2000; Carlson et al., 2010; Nakashole et al., 2011; Huang and Riloff, 2013). Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.
